data.targetWord: a ruling family or line of rulers that governed China for a period of time

examples.en-GB: The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 until it was replaced by the Qing dynasty in 1644.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the supreme ruler of imperial China, seen as holding authority over the whole empire

examples.en-GB: The Qianlong Emperor ruled Qing China at a time of great power and territorial expansion.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the traditional Chinese idea that a ruler had the right to govern if they maintained order and prosperity; disasters or rebellion could suggest the mandate had been lost

examples.en-GB: Rebels used the idea of the Mandate of Heaven to justify overthrowing a dynasty they said had lost the right to rule.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the system of government officials who carried out laws, collected taxes, kept records and advised rulers

examples.en-GB: China's large bureaucracy allowed the emperor to govern an enormous empire through thousands of trained officials.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: competitive tests used to select government officials in imperial China, focusing on Confucian texts, essay writing and moral reasoning

examples.en-GB: A young man who passed the civil service examinations could gain a position in the imperial government.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a system of ideas emphasising order, respect for authority, family duty, moral behaviour, education and good government, linked to the thinker Confucius

examples.en-GB: Confucianism shaped how officials were expected to behave and how the civil service examinations were structured.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a Qing policy limiting most Western trade to the port of Canton (Guangzhou) and requiring foreign merchants to deal through approved Chinese traders

examples.en-GB: Under the Canton system, British merchants could only trade at one port and had to follow strict rules about where they could live.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a powerful addictive drug made from poppies, sold by British merchants into China in the nineteenth century, causing serious social and political problems

examples.en-GB: The large-scale sale of opium into China drained silver from the country and undermined Qing authority.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a treaty forced on a weaker state by a stronger power, giving unfair advantages to the stronger side

examples.en-GB: The Treaty of Nanjing was an unequal treaty that forced China to open ports to British trade and cede Hong Kong.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a state's right to control its own territory, laws and decisions without outside interference

examples.en-GB: The Opium Wars and unequal treaties weakened Chinese sovereignty by forcing Qing rulers to accept foreign demands.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a fine, hard type of pottery, often made into bowls, plates and vases; Chinese porcelain was prized across the world for its quality

examples.en-GB: European buyers paid high prices for Chinese porcelain because it was technically superior to what could be made in Europe at the time.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a Ming admiral who led large voyages across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433, demonstrating Chinese maritime power and diplomatic reach

examples.en-GB: Zheng He's voyages reached East Africa and showed that China had major sea connections long before European empires expanded.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: gifts or goods offered to a ruler or state as part of diplomatic relations, showing respect or acknowledgement of authority

examples.en-GB: Foreign rulers sent tribute to the Chinese emperor as part of diplomatic relationships during the Ming period.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the large imperial palace complex in Beijing, centre of Ming and Qing political and ceremonial life, restricted to ordinary people

examples.en-GB: The Forbidden City was built during the Ming dynasty and symbolised the emperor's power at the heart of the empire.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the Qing official sent to Canton in 1839 to suppress the opium trade; he confiscated and destroyed British opium stocks, triggering the First Opium War

examples.en-GB: Lin Zexu's destruction of opium in Canton became a symbol of Chinese resistance to the illegal drug trade.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the 1842 agreement ending the First Opium War, under which China ceded Hong Kong to Britain, paid compensation and opened additional ports to trade

examples.en-GB: The Treaty of Nanjing was one of the first of the unequal treaties that weakened Qing authority over trade and territory.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the dynasty that ruled China from 1644 to 1912, founded by the Manchus from northeast Asia

examples.en-GB: The Qing dynasty ruled for over two and a half centuries before revolution ended imperial rule in China in 1912.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the dynasty that ruled China from 1368 to 1644, known for strong central government, the Forbidden City, porcelain production and Zheng He's voyages

examples.en-GB: The Ming dynasty rebuilt China after Mongol rule and created the Forbidden City as its imperial centre.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the management of relationships and negotiations between states or rulers

examples.en-GB: Lord Macartney's 1793 embassy to China was a diplomatic mission to seek expanded trading rights for Britain.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a historian's or writer's explanation of past events; interpretations can differ because people use different evidence or ask different questions

examples.en-GB: Some historians interpret the Opium Wars mainly as trade conflicts; others focus on them as examples of European imperial aggression.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the ranking of groups in society from those with the most status and power to those with the least

examples.en-GB: In imperial China the social hierarchy placed scholars and officials at the top, followed by farmers, artisans and merchants.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: farming; the cultivation of crops and rearing of animals to produce food

examples.en-GB: Most people in Ming and Qing China worked in agriculture, growing crops such as rice, wheat and tea.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: something that stays the same over time, even as other aspects of history change

examples.en-GB: The civil service examination system showed continuity because it survived from the Ming through the Qing period.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a port city in China that was opened to foreign trade and residence under unequal treaties after the Opium Wars

examples.en-GB: Shanghai became one of China's main treaty ports, where foreign nationals had special legal privileges.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the war fought between Britain and Qing China from 1839 to 1842 over trade, the opium trade and Chinese sovereignty, ending in Chinese defeat

examples.en-GB: The First Opium War ended with the Treaty of Nanjing, which gave Britain significant trade and territorial advantages over China.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the importance of a person, event or development, judged by its scale, impact and long-term effects

examples.en-GB: Historians debate the significance of Zheng He's voyages: some see them as evidence of China's global power, others focus on why the voyages stopped.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: the British diplomatic mission of 1793 sent to Qing China to seek expanded trading rights, which failed to achieve Britain's main aims

examples.en-GB: The failure of the Macartney embassy showed that Qing China was not willing to accept British demands for open trade on British terms.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a valuable fabric made from silkworm threads; one of China's most important export goods across Asia and Europe

examples.en-GB: Chinese silk was traded along overland and maritime routes and was highly prized in European markets.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a reason why something happened; historians look for multiple causes that together explain an event or development

examples.en-GB: The causes of the First Opium War included trade disputes, the opium trade, and Britain's desire to challenge Chinese control over commerce.

topics: Imperial China and the Wider World

data.targetWord: a result or effect of an event; historians consider both short-term and long-term consequences

examples.en-GB: One consequence of the unequal treaties was that Qing China lost control over certain ports and legal rights over foreign citizens.
